title: ASIC suspends Melbourne AFSL, reports FY26 enforcement outcomes
full_text:
ASIC has suspended the AFSL of a Melbourne-based wealth and trustee firm for six months.
The AFSL of Central Accord, which is based in Cremorne, was suspended from 30 July 2026 to 4 February 2027.
The firm’s activities first came to ASIC’s attention after it failed to pay invoices to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) for more than 12 months. This saw Central Accord expelled as an AFCA member, a requirement of holding an AFSL.
The regulator subsequently stated Central Accord is no longer carrying on a financial services business.
If Central Accord Pty Ltd is in a position to recommence its financial services business before the expiration of the suspension, ASIC said, it may make submissions to ASIC requesting that the suspension order be revoked.
Central Accord Pty Ltd may also apply to the Administrative Review Tribunal (ART) for a review of ASIC’s decision.
In July, ASIC temporarily suspended the AFSL of Prime Value Asset Management until 7 August after the firm failed to meet its audit and reporting lodgement obligations. The AFS licence was suspended because Prime Value failed to meet its statutory audit and financial reporting lodgement obligations for the company for the financial years ending 2024 and 2025.
ASIC also found Prime Value had previously failed to meet financial resource requirements and lodge compliance plan audit reports for some of its retail schemes, however these breaches have been rectified.
ASIC has since reinstated Prime Value’s AFSL.
Later that month, ASIC cancelled the AFSL of a managed investment scheme responsible entity following a payment by the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort (CSLR). Queensland-based Australian Fiduciaries received a determination from the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) which it failed to pay.
Australian Fiduciaries was the responsible entity of three registered managed investment schemes – the Global Diversified Alpha Fund, the Global Multi-Strategy Fund and the Global All Seasons Fund.
FY2025/26 results
The regulator has also detailed its activities from the 2025/26 financial year, including delivering 150 administrative enforcement outcomes across the financial, credit and corporate sectors.
This marked the highest level of removals and restrictions by ASIC in the past five years, as well as seeing a sharp rise in disqualifications during this period.
ASIC enforcement activity
Source: ASIC, August 2026
It found that six in 10 (61 per cent) financial services outcomes resulting in a permanent banning or licence cancellation, while the large majority (89 per cent) of credit-related instances ended with a similar result.
Tallying up the year, ASIC issued 77 permanent banning or cancellations within credit and financial services, with 31 against individuals and 46 for organisations.
Of these, six were hit with a 10-year ban and 31 were banned for less than years. Among the 36 director disqualifications in FY26, 18 received the maximum period of five years available under the Corporations Act.
The regulator also noted the banning of 15 advisers linked to the Shield Master Fund or the First Guardian Master Fund in FY26, as well as taking further action against licensees, a director of a licensee and a responsible manager.
ASIC chair Sarah Court said: “Every banning order, licence cancellation and director disqualification removes a pathway for rogue operators to continue earning a living from misconduct. By removing high-risk participants from the market, we are disrupting misconduct at its source and making it harder for those who disregard the law to continue operating.”
The ability to ban or suspend those it believes are engaging in misconduct is particularly important, Court said, because it allows them to halt activities faster than standard legal proceeding allow – such as through the courts – which can “help prevent further harm, drive behavioural change and strengthen trust and confidence in Australia’s financial and corporate markets”.
“ASIC will continue to take decisive action against individuals and businesses that fail to meet their legal obligations. Administrative enforcement outcomes are a powerful way to protect consumers and investors, deter misconduct and maintain confidence in Australia’s financial, credit and corporate markets.
“If you misuse a position of trust, fail to meet your obligations or engage in misconduct, ASIC can and will act to remove you from the market.”
author: Shy-Ann Arkinstall
